transcript.text: I've just bought an AEG L7FEE865R and the Eco 40-60 wash says 3:39 and seems to take forever. My old machine did a 40 wash in an hour. Is it faulty? Should I send it back?

No — a displayed 3:39 on Eco 40-60 is normally not a fault and, by itself, is not a reason to send the machine back. Eco 40-60 cycles commonly take around 3–4 hours: they use less energy by heating more gently and washing for longer. The time can also alter as the machine weighs the load and manages foam and spin balance. Your old one-hour 40°C wash was likely a standard or quick programme, rather than the energy-saving Eco 40-60 cycle. For ordinary laundry, use the normal 40°C programme or a quick programme when suitable; Eco 40-60 is chiefly the efficiency-test/energy-saving setting, not the fastest everyday wash. It would be worth querying as a fault only if the programme does not finish, the remaining time repeatedly goes back up, an error code appears, or it is still stuck with water in the drum. Has it completed normally at roughly that time?
Yes, it finishes and spins fine, and the clothes come out clean. It really does take about 3h40 every time on Eco 40-60, though. The Cottons 40 shows about 2 hours. No error codes.

That suggests it is behaving normally, not showing a fault. A consistent roughly 3 hour 40 minute Eco 40-60 cycle that completes, spins properly, leaves clean clothes and shows no errors is exactly the pattern expected from an energy-saving programme. The roughly two-hour Cottons 40 setting is the better comparison with a conventional everyday 40°C wash. Use that when you want a shorter normal cycle; use Eco 40-60 when lowest energy use matters more than time. There is no reason to send it back on this symptom alone. It would only become worth reporting if it started failing to finish, repeatedly added substantial time, left water in the drum, produced errors, or stopped heating/cleaning properly.

candidates: Normal Eco 40-60 programme duration and automatic time adjustment (high)
Cycle time extending due to load sensing, foam or an imbalance correction (low)
